chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Uqba ibn Muhammad, from Salama ibn Muhammad, the cap-seller, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) passed by a man who had raised his voice against a man, demanding something trivial from him. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'For how much are you demanding from him?' He said: 'For such and such.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Has it not reached you that it has been said: There is no religion for the one who has no muru'a (magnanimity/dignity)?'

key_terms.دِين: Religion/faith — here used to mean the genuine substance of religious commitment, not merely outward practice
key_terms.مُرُوءَة: Muru'a — a comprehensive virtue encompassing magnanimity, dignity, generosity, and noble character; the quality of a truly noble person who would not demean others or act miserly
key_terms.يَسِير: Trivial/small — emphasizing that the debt or claim was minor, making the public scene even more inappropriate

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Sadiq say about muru'a (magnanimity) and its relation to religion?
ai.summary: Imam Sadiq (peace be upon him) witnesses a man publicly shaming another over a trivial debt and intervenes by reminding him of a well-known saying that lacking muru'a — the virtuous quality of magnanimity, dignity, and generosity — invalidates one's religious standing. The term muru'a in classical Islamic ethics signified the noble character expected of a free person: composure, generosity, and refusing to humiliate others over petty matters. This teaching connects proper social conduct with the validity of one's faith itself.
